question: What is the meaning of information about design for disassembly in relation to product information, component information, design specifications?
data_group: product information, component information, design specifications
description: The information about design for disassembly (DfD) in relation to product information, component information, and design specifications is crucial for sustainable construction. It helps to ensure that products can be easily disassembled, reused, or recycled at the end of their life cycle, reducing waste and promoting a circular economy. The four criteria for DfD, as mentioned in the context, include connection type, connection accessibility, type of crossings, and type of form containment. These criteria are used to evaluate the potential for DfD and to develop a scoring system that quantifies the ability to recover the product and assess its future use in another building project. The material composition section in the Construction Materials Passport (CMP) is also linked to the performance score, which is calculated in the DfD section. This information is essential for designing products that are more sustainable and environmentally friendly.

The parameter “Design for disassembly” (DfD) is characterized through four criteria, as obtained 
from [9]: (1) Connection type, (2) Type of connection accessibility, (3) Type of crossings, and (4) Type 
of form containment. A scoring system allows to quantify the ability to recover the product and to assess 
its future use in another building project. The system rating is from 0 to 1 (or 0 to100%) with 1 being 
the best. Based on the scoring of the four indicators, the potential DfD can be evaluated. Different 
categories from the literature [22–24] were compared and merged for a refined set of sub-criteria for the 
four DfD criteria, as shown in Table 5.

The parameter “Material composition” requires a predefined set of material types, which was adapted 
from the list of material types used in the Bill of Quantities in Level(s) to include all relevant types: (1) 
Concrete, brick (stone), tiles and ceramics; (2) Structural wood or other bio-based; (3) Glass; (4) Plastic; 
(5) Bituminous mixtures; (6) Metal; (7) Insulation materials; (8) Gypsum; (9) Mixture.  
The material composition section in the CMP is linked to the performance score, which is calculated 
in the DfD section. The smaller the disassembly performance score, the less likely it is to know the 
material composition at the product component level. In this case, it is important to estimate the material 
composition at the total product level. The total sum of the materials must amount to 100%. 
4.  Conclusions and outlook 
This paper wants to support the standardization of a CMP in the construction sector. However, for a 
large-scale use of this tool, and for ensuring a level-playing field, regulations must be put in place by 
the competent authorities or through voluntary schemes by significant business associations, such as the 
European Construction Technology Platform (ECTP). 
A set of CMP for products can be adapted to constitute a Building Materials Passport (BMP). The
